catalog_quote: Stress in UNT is phonemic and serves both to differentiate between words of different lexical classes and to mark person-aspectual distinctions on certain classes of verb. In general, stress is placed on the final syllable of words that end in a long vowel or a closed syllable, and (except in verbs) on the penultimate syllable of words ending in a short vowel. The stress on verbs is always on the final syllable, with the exception of verbs in the perfective aspect or in the second person, in which case the stress falls on the penultimate syllable. The principal phonetic correlates of stress in UNT are increased duration and, to a lesser extent, amplitude of the syllabic nucleus, stressed short vowels being realized with the same duration as long vowels. new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is on the final syllable when it is heavy (long vowel or closed); a light (short open) final syllable throws stress to the penult. Verbs override this: they are stressed on the final syllable regardless, except perfective and second-person forms, which are penultimate. Stress is therefore weight-driven in nouns and other classes and morphologically fixed in verbs; the same rule is repeated verbatim in García-Vega & Tucker 2021: 55-74 (p. 59) with citation to Beck 2011.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in Beck 2004 §1.3. Ideophones 'have no word-level stress and all syllables seem to be given equal prosodic weight' (Beck 2004, p. 34; cf. García-Vega & Tucker 2021: 59 'no fixed primary stress', though out of context they are stressed by the regular pattern).
new_statements.exceptions: Rule hedged 'In general'. Verbs: always final except perfective aspect and second person (penult). Prosodic apophony nominalization shifts the accent to the penult and laryngealizes the final vowel (Beck 2004 §2.3.8.2, pp. 88-89; a few cases laryngealize without accent shift). Ideophones lack word-level stress. One tonal minimal pair (tša:án 'ant' vs tšaá:n 'ripe') arises from stress on a long vowel giving a rising contour. García-Vega & Tucker 2021: 59 say patterns are 'predictable and regular notwithstanding a few exceptions (Beck 2011)'. Phonetic correlates: duration first, amplitude second; short stressed vowels lengthen to long-vowel duration; instrumentally confirmed with added f0 rise and quality shift (García-Vega & Tucker) and higher H1-H2 (Puderbaugh 2019).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, phonemic (contrasts lexical class and person/aspect on verbs). The only phrase-level prosody noted is a rising intonation marking yes/no questions (§1.3, §3.1.3). Data from both the Patla and Chicontla dialects of UNT.
new_statements.identity_note: Beck's data come from the Patla and Chicontla dialects of Upper Necaxa Totonac (both under uppe1275; no separate glottocodes). The Glottolog 'grammar' entry (Beck 2000, Linguistic Typology) is an adjective-typology article, not a grammar; the real descriptions are Beck 2004 (sketch) and Beck 2011 (dictionary with grammatical introduction).

sources.locator: §1.3 'Stress, tone, and prosody', p. 4 of the author's PDF (PDF page 9); printed LINCOM pagination may differ
sources.note: §1.3 'Stress, tone, and prosody' (printed p. 4, PDF p. 9): stress is phonemic; final syllable if word ends in long vowel or closed syllable, otherwise penult (except verbs); verbs always final except perfective / 2nd person which are penult; correlates duration > amplitude; one tonal minimal pair; ideophones have no word-level stress (p. 34); prosodic apophony nominalization shifts accent to penult + final laryngealization (§2.3.8.2, pp. 88-89).

Journal of the International Phonetic Association 51(1): 55-74. doi:10.1017/S0025100318000439 (author accepted version, University of Alberta ERA handle 123456789/29486)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: p. 59 (PDF p. 5): 'Stress patterns are predictable and regular notwithstanding a few exceptions (Beck 2011). Stress falls on the final syllable of words that end in a long vowel, e.g. pi'ta:jú.. or a closed syllable, like chojót.. or the penultimate syllable of words ending in a short vowel as in pó:ti'; ideophones have no fixed primary stress. Instrumental: stress cued by increased duration, higher f0 and a shift in vowel quality (lower/backer); short stressed vowels lengthen, long stressed vowels not consistently longer.
